segments.answerShort: Yes, about 20 inches is the figure recalled for the proposed successor.

segments.title: An armoured target ship for gunnery trials
segments.body: In an earlier game, one player gave a battleship about 35 inches of armour all around and a single 9-inch gun. Its purpose was to serve as a gunnery target for other designs. In a trial with destroyers, their ammunition ran out before the battleship sank. That left the number needed to sink it unresolved.

evidence.note: A player recalls using a heavily armoured, lightly armed battleship as a target and exhausting the attacking destroyers' ammunition.

segments.summary: A deliberately over-armoured game ship puts the attacking destroyers' ammunition reserves to the test.

segments.title: Do slow 20-inch guns justify 8-inch secondaries?
segments.body: The builder fits quadruple 6-inch mounts to the battleship. A viewer suggests that an 8-inch secondary battery might earn its place during the long reload of the main guns. Even allowing for that interval, the builder considers the existing 6-inch mounts adequate.

evidence.note: The builder chooses quadruple 6-inch mounts and favours adding more of them.
The slow rate of fire of 20-inch guns gives the proposed 8-inch battery some justification. Both participants accept that 6-inch guns suffice.

segments.summary: A battleship fitted with quadruple 6-inch mounts prompts a proposal for 8-inch secondaries to cover the long interval between its 20-inch salvoes.
segments.question: Does the slow rate of fire of a 20-inch main battery make 8-inch secondary guns worthwhile?
segments.answerShort: It makes the option more defensible, but 6-inch secondaries are still considered sufficient.

segments.title: Testing 20.9-inch guns against a heavy cruiser
segments.body: The simulated heavy cruiser carries 14 inches of armour and single 10-inch guns. Several battleship shots land beyond it. When the cruiser sinks, one player credits a single salvo. Another specifies that just one 20.9-inch shell hit.

evidence.note: Several shots overshoot the heavy cruiser before it sinks. One player distinguishes the single shell that hit from the whole salvo.

segments.summary: The 20.9-inch game battleship overshoots several times before a single shell sinks the opposing heavy cruiser.

segments.title: Mixed batteries and protection on a British pre-dreadnought
segments.body: The pre-dreadnought hull leaves little room for the tower and funnel. An attempt at 21 knots ends with a more modest 18-knot target. The ship needs to withstand blast from its own guns, and its deck armour has a separate job against plunging fire. Once the design reaches its target weight, the inner deck still has substantial protection.

evidence.note: The 1890 gun limit prompts a switch to 1895. The build takes 9.2-inch side guns and 4-inch secondaries, then drops from 21 knots to 18.
The design reaches its target weight, and the inner deck retains substantial armour.

segments.summary: The British designer caps the largest gun at 12 inches in 1890. Moving the date to 1895 opens up the mixed battery requested for this pre-dreadnought.
segments.question: Could the British pre-dreadnought in the request be built with the game's 1890 equipment?
segments.answerShort: The 1890 designer stops at 12-inch guns. The build moves to 1895 and pairs 9.2-inch side guns with 4-inch secondaries.

segments.title: A dense 6-inch broadside at close range
segments.body: Each of the eight mounts on the engaged side held three guns, giving a nominal 24-gun broadside. The player credited that concentration of fire with the opponent's trouble once it closed to secondary range. The example comes from an earlier battle with a different design.

evidence.note: A player recalls eight triple 6-inch mounts on each side of the battleships in an earlier engagement.

segments.summary: An opponent in a player's earlier game came within range of a battleship carrying eight triple 6-inch mounts per side.

segments.title: Mixed-calibre gunnery and torpedo range
segments.body: Shells of different sizes are already in the air, although few hits are expected until the ships get closer. The player's pre-dreadnought can still use its guns at the present distance. Closing further for a torpedo attack holds little appeal in this particular fight.

evidence.note: Several calibres are firing. The player expects few hits at first and keeps the ship outside torpedo range.

segments.summary: In the simulated pre-dreadnought duel, both sides open fire with several calibres well before the ships come into torpedo range.

segments.title: Fleet size versus research spending in the campaign
segments.body: Building fewer ships left money for research, provided the player could win battles with the fleet already afloat. Players also remember the economy in that version of the campaign as erratic. One recalls reaching the dreadnought stage with 14-inch guns already available to the first generation of ships.

evidence.note: A player recalls problems with the older campaign economy and a first generation of dreadnoughts armed with 14-inch guns.
Building fewer ships freed money for research, on the assumption that the existing fleet could still do the fighting.

segments.summary: A player recalls how building fewer ships left money for research in an earlier Ultimate Admiral: Dreadnoughts campaign.

segments.title: A British reworking of the Lexington battlecruiser
segments.body: The requested calibre is 16.5 inches, and Lexington supplies the starting hull. Triple turrets were already familiar to American designers in the period imagined for the ship. In the game, a lower speed target and geared turbines free enough displacement to improve the armour. Accepting an awkward forward gun arrangement leaves a little weight for the main belt.

evidence.note: The request specifies a British reworking and a 16.5-inch calibre. Lexington is chosen as the starting point.
The build carries little armour despite its excess weight. American use of triple turrets comes up as the guns are reconsidered.
Regular crew spacing, a 33-knot target and geared turbines free weight for protection.
Accepting the forward gun arrangement leaves room for a small increase in main-belt armour.

segments.summary: A viewer asks for a British take on an American battlecruiser with 16.5-inch guns. The first Lexington build is already overweight with very little armour.
segments.question: What would a British reworking of an American battlecruiser with 16.5-inch guns look like?
segments.answerShort: The game design starts from Lexington, trades speed for armour and keeps a forward gun arrangement the designer would have preferred to change.

segments.title: Finding weight for armour on the Lexington build
segments.body: The first savings come from reverting to regular crew spacing. Lowering the speed to 33 knots still leaves the simulated battlecruiser about 4,000 tons over its limit. Geared turbines move it below the limit, freeing several thousand tons for armour and allowing the ship's balance to be adjusted. The 5-inch secondaries go into twin mounts, with twelve guns counted in all.

evidence.note: At 33 knots the model is still about 4,000 tons overweight. With geared turbines it has spare weight for armour and 5-inch secondaries.

segments.summary: Geared turbines free several thousand tons in the game after a speed cut alone leaves Lexington overweight.

segments.title: Heavy-shell penetration in the Lexington trial
segments.body: The two battlecruisers exchange fire. The opposing ship appears to carry thicker armour than Lexington. One of Lexington's heavy shells penetrates shortly before the game demonstration ends, while the outcome of the duel is still open.

evidence.note: Lexington retains its secondary guns for the trial. Its opponent has the heavier armour, and one of Lexington's main-battery shells penetrates.

segments.summary: The simulated Lexington faces a battlecruiser with heavier armour and scores a penetrating hit with its main battery.
